title: Counting Invocations in a Call Tree
quickIdea: Write the recurrence the code implies, then tabulate from the base cases upward. Counting calls by expanding the tree by hand is how marks are lost.
remember: If a function makes two recursive calls on n-1 and n-3, the number of activations satisfies T(n) = 1 + T(n-1) + T(n-3) for n >= 1, with T(n) = 1 for every n below the threshold, because a call that returns immediately is still an invocation.

GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.39: the table is T(0..6) = 1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 17, 25, so get(6) is invoked 25 times. Only 12 of those activations reach the printf, because the 13 calls with n < 1 return at the first line.
'How many times is the function invoked' includes the call from main; 'how many recursive calls are made' is one less. GATE's options are usually one apart for exactly this reason.

GATE CSE 2018 Q.45: Count(1024,1024) halves x ten times for each of the 1023 values of y, so the print runs 10 x 1023 = 10230 times. Two parameters moving at different rates give a product, not a sequence.
A call-count recurrence and a time-complexity recurrence are not the same object: the count keeps a +1 for every activation, the complexity keeps the work done in one activation.
Tabulate bottom-up whenever the arguments only decrease. Each entry needs only entries already computed, and the exam arithmetic stays small.

example.prompt: void get(int n) { if (n < 1) return; get(n-1); get(n-3); printf("%d", n); } How many times is get invoked by get(6), and how many digits are printed?
example.work: T(n) = 1 + T(n-1) + T(n-3) for n >= 1 and T(n) = 1 below it: T(0)=1, T(1)=3, T(2)=5, T(3)=7, T(4)=11, T(5)=17, T(6)=25. Of the 25 activations, the 13 with n < 1 print nothing, so 25 - 13 = 12 digits are printed.

gateAngle: Both counting questions of this decade are tabulation questions: 2015 Set 3 Q.39 is a one-dimensional table and 2018 Q.45 is a product of two rates. Neither needs the tree drawn.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.39: how many times is get invoked by get(6)?
variations.why: The recurrence counts the base calls too, and adds one for the call from main.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: For the same get function, how many invocations does get(5) make, and how many digits does it print?
variations.why: T(5) = 17 by the same table; the calls with n < 1 among those 17 are 9, leaving 8 prints.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is a call with n = 0 counted as an invocation in the 2015 question?
variations.answer: Because the function is entered: the return happens inside the function, after the frame is created. The question asks how many times get is invoked, not how many times it prints.
variations.why: This is the distinction between the 25 of 2015 Q.39 and the 12 prints of the same program.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Count(x, y) halves x and decrements y as in GATE CSE 2018 Q.45. If the initial call were Count(1024, 512), how many stars are printed?
variations.answer: 5110: ten stars for each y from 512 down to 2, that is 511 values.
variations.why: The same product of a logarithmic rate and a linear rate, with one of the numbers changed.

trap.what: Counting only the leaf calls, or only the calls that print, when the question asks for invocations.
trap.why: A recursion's activation count includes every frame created, and the base-case frames are created too. The number that prints is smaller by exactly the number of base calls.
trap.counterexample: In get(6) the invocation count is 25 but the printf runs 12 times; an answer of 12 or of 13 comes from counting one class of frame only.

check.question: void f(int n) { if (n == 0) return; f(n-1); f(n-1); } How many invocations does f(3) make?
check.explanation: T(n) = 1 + 2T(n-1) with T(0) = 1, so T(3) = 1 + 2(1 + 2(1 + 2 x 1)) = 15. The call tree is a complete binary tree of depth 3: 8 leaves and 7 internal nodes.
